lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Bedtime for Giants. Read very slowly, so the ends arrive gently.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Shh.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: This is Bedtime for Giants.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: This is Nanny Bramblewick. Close your eyes, dear. Both of them. All of them, Agnes.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: This is The Long Lullaby. Pull the quilt up to your chin, dear. Gently. Mind the village.

lines.speaker: Bartholomew, a Giant
lines.text: Nanny? I can't sleep. My feet are in the next county, and they're cold.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Then we'll ask the next county to put a blanket over them, dear.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: There. Better?

lines.speaker: Bartholomew, a Giant
lines.text: ...Better.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Goodnight, Bartholomew.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Very Early Stories. It isn't morning, dear. It's only thinking about it. Lie back down.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Hush, now. The birds aren't up. The sun's not up. Even the kettle's asleep.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: The only ones awake are you, and the operator on that little ship, out between the stations. Wave, if you like. They can't see you. It's still nice.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: The Afternoon Nap. Draw the curtains, dear. They're about a mile each. Take your time.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: A giant's nap is a serious matter. Little Agnes napped last spring, and when she woke up, there was a village on her knee.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: They were very nice about it. They held a fete, and asked her to open it, and she did. Very carefully. With one finger.

clips.title: The Mountain Who Wanted a Hat

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Once upon a time, there was a mountain who wanted a hat.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: All the other mountains had snow on top, white and neat, like a good wool hat. But this was a low, round sort of mountain, and the snow never stayed. Every winter it slid off, and went to live in the valley.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: So the mountain asked the clouds. Excuse me, it said, in its slow, stony voice. Would one of you sit on my head? Just for a while?

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: And a small grey cloud, who had nowhere in particular to be, said: all right.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: And it sat there, on the mountain's head, all afternoon, and all evening. And the mountain felt very smart, and very warm, and a little bit...

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Oh. He's asleep.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Goodnight, Bartholomew. There's a cloud on your head, dear. Leave it. It's company.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Once upon a time, a giant found a very small moon. It was sitting in a field, about the size of a turnip, glowing a little, and looking lost.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Are you a moon, said the giant. I'm trying to be, said the moon. But I've come down too far, and I don't know the way back up.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: So the giant took it home in his pocket, and put it on the windowsill by his bed. And every night it glowed, just enough to see the edge of the quilt by.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Some nights it was full, and some nights it was only a little slice, because it didn't want to be any trouble.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: And the giant would look at the moon, and the moon would look at the giant, and they'd both think: well. This is nice. And slowly, very slowly, the giant's eyes...

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: There. Goodnight, Agnes. Leave the moon on.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: There was once a giant who couldn't sleep, so he counted sheep.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Now, sheep are very small, to a giant, so he needed a great many. He counted a thousand, and then ten thousand, and he wasn't the least bit tired. But the sheep were. They'd been going over that fence all night.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: So the oldest sheep, whose name was Margery, stopped at the top of the fence, and turned round, and began to count the giant.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: One giant, said Margery.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: One giant.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: One giant.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: It's very restful, being counted. It means somebody has noticed you're there, and that you're one, and that one is enough.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: One giant.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Goodnight.

clips.title: The Giant Who Hid Too Well

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Once there was a giant who loved hide and seek, but was very bad at it, being about the size of a hill.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: He'd hide behind a forest, and his head would stick out of the top. He'd hide behind a lake, and everyone could see his knees.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: So one day he lay down in a field, and kept very still. So still that grass grew on him. So still that a sheep wandered up his arm, and a little path wore across his tummy, and a family came and had a picnic on his knee.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: And nobody found him. Not for years. And he lay there, very happy, listening to the picnics.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: He won, in the end. He's still winning, actually.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Shh. Don't tell anyone where he is.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: There was once a lighthouse who told bedtime stories to the ships.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: It didn't have a voice, so it told them with its light. One flash for each word. Very slowly. Out across the dark water.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Once.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Upon.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: A.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Time.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: It took a very long time to tell a story that way. The ships didn't mind. They rocked on the water, and watched the light come round, and waited for the next word, the way you wait for the next breath.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Nobody ever found out how the stories ended. Not one ship. They were always asleep by the fourth word.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Very sensible, ships.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: A giant's slippers are very large, and very old, and very patient.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Every night they wait by the bed, side by side, like two warm boats tied up in a harbour. And every night, the giant steps out of them and climbs into bed, and the slippers stay where they are, keeping each other company.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: They talk a little, once the lights are out. The left one worries about the stairs. The right one says, he always manages. And he does.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: And when the rain comes, like tonight, they listen to it on the window, and they think: we're inside. We're together. The feet will be back in the morning.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: That's all slippers want, really.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Now. Where were we.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Ah, yes. The giant was walking home.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Tonight's story is about a giant on his way to bed. It's a long way. Lie still. We'll walk with him.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Once, not very long ago, a giant set off home after a long day of being enormous.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: He walked past a forest so old it had forgotten it was a forest, and thought it was a crowd. A very tall, very quiet crowd, waiting for something nice to happen.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: He tiptoed past. Giants can tiptoe. It takes about a week.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: He stepped over a river. It was a small river, and he was a large giant, so he stepped over it the way you would step over a ribbon.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: The river said thank you. Rivers are very polite, if you don't stand in them.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: He passed a village with all its lights out but one. In the one lit window, a girl was reading under a blanket with a torch.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: He bent down, very slowly, and blew the curtains closed. Just a little breath. Like this.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Goodnight, girl with the torch.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: An owl landed on his shoulder, and asked where he was going. Home, said the giant. The owl said that sounded nice, and stayed for the ride.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Owls are good company. They don't talk much. Now and then they say who, to keep you on your toes.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: The clouds came down low to see who was walking, and he walked right through them, and for a while he couldn't see his own feet.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: That's all right, he thought. They know the way.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: He counted the stars as he walked. He got to eleven thousand, and lost his place, and had to start again.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: He didn't mind. It's a good thing, to have something to count that never runs out.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: And by then, he was nearly home.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: And so are you. Goodnight.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: And then he yawned. Such a big yawn that the wind turned round.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Goodnight, giant. Goodnight, you.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: We'll find out what happened next tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: We never do. Sleep well.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: I've been reading to giants for a very long time, dear, and I have never once finished a story.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Nobody has ever stayed awake for one. I think that's the nicest thing a story can do.

clips.title: A Forecast for the Very Large

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: A forecast for the very large. A light breeze tonight, from the east. That's Bartholomew, breathing out.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Then a light breeze from the west. That's Bartholomew, breathing in. Mind your hats.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Settling by morning. Snoring in the hills, later. Nothing to worry about.

clips.title: The Ghost Who Was Too Small

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Once upon a time, a very small ghost went to haunt a giant.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: It floated up the stairs, which took most of the night, and into the giant's bedroom, and it said: boo.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: The giant didn't hear. So the ghost said it again, louder. Boo.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: The giant opened one enormous eye, and looked at the ghost, and said: oh. A moth. And went back to sleep.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: The ghost was very offended. But it was also very tired, after all those stairs, and the lampshade looked warm. So it curled up inside. Just for a minute.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: It lives there now. It keeps the light soft. Some nights it says boo, very quietly, to itself, just to keep its hand in.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Goodnight, little ghost.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: It's nearly Halloween, so if you see a very large sheet walking about the valley this week, please don't be frightened.

lines.speaker: Little Agnes, a Giant
lines.text: Nanny? I can't find my nightie.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: That's only Agnes.

clips.title: The Convergence: A Moon Goes Missing

lines.speaker: Little Agnes, a Giant
lines.text: Nanny, a moon's gone.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Has it, dear?

lines.speaker: Little Agnes, a Giant
lines.text: Everyone says so.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Then it's gone to bed. Which is where you are. Goodnight, Agnes.

lines.speaker: Bartholomew, a Giant
lines.text: Nanny... I can smell toast.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Everyone can, dear. Close your eyes, and it'll be breakfast in the morning.

clips.title: The Convergence: The Song Nobody Can Finish

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: There's a little song going round tonight. Nobody knows the end of it.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Which is the very best kind, for bedtime. Shh.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Three little knocks at the bedroom door. Nobody there.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Just a dream, knocking a bit early. Let it in when you're ready, dear.

clips.title: The Convergence: A Colour With No Name

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: The sky went a colour just now, dears. There isn't a word for it.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: It's a colour for sleeping. You only see it with your eyes closed.

lines.speaker: Little Agnes, a Giant
lines.text: Nanny, there's a pigeon in the village. On my knee.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Is it a nice pigeon?

lines.speaker: Little Agnes, a Giant
lines.text: It knows everyone.

lines.speaker: Nanny Bramblewick
lines.text: Then it can stay. Goodnight, pigeon.
